item.title: Nutrients in food mimic calorie restrictions. Can they improve our health?
item.description: Research in humans has yet to show that compounds reproduce the effects of calorie restriction or extend healthspan.
item.content:encoded:
Scroll through social media and you will soon encounter advice about living longer, from fasting plans and supplements to elaborate daily routines. Yet reaching an advanced age tells us little about how healthy or independent those later years will be.

Researchers often use the term healthspan for the years spent in good health, free from disability or chronic disease. In 2021, global life expectancy was 71.4 years, while healthy life expectancy was 61.9 years, according to the World Health Organization (WHO). That represents a gap of nine and a half years. A separate analysis estimated that this gap widened in 203 of 204 countries and territories between 1990 and 2023.

The WHO takes a broader view of healthy ageing, focusing on the abilities that allow people to do what they value, such as undertaking daily tasks, maintaining relationships and contributing to society. This recognises that people can live well while managing a health condition. “Functional healthspan” describes how long someone maintains the capacities needed for independent living.

As we age, declining muscle strength and mass, reduced aerobic fitness and even “inflammaging” (or low-grade inflammation) become more prevalent. These changes vary considerably between people. Diet, physical activity and sleep can influence how well we age, although income, housing, healthcare and the wider environment also play important roles.

item.title: Mumbai: Six allegedly undocumented Bangladeshi immigrants arrested
item.description: They have been accused of providing forged Aadhaar and other identity documents to Bangladeshi citizens to help them enter India.
item.content:encoded:
Six allegedly undocumented Bangladeshi migrants were arrested in Mumbai, ANI quoted the police as saying on Friday.

The six persons have been accused of providing forged Aadhaar and other identity documents to Bangladeshi citizens to help them enter India, ANI reported.

Forty forged Aadhaar cards, Permanent Account Number cards, railway tickets with QR codes and other Indian identity documents were recovered from them, the news agency quoted the Mumbai Police as saying.

Since the terror attack in Jammu and Kashmir’s Pahalgam in April 2025, the police in several states, most of them ruled by the Bharatiya Janata Party, have been detaining Bengali-speaking persons – mostly Muslims – and asking them to prove that they are Indian citizens.

Several persons have been forced into Bangladesh after they allegedly could not prove their Indian citizenship. In some cases, persons who were mistakenly sent to Bangladesh returned to the country after state authorities in India proved that they were Indians.

Scroll has also reported on several cases of persons who were forced into Bangladesh being brought back to India, as the authorities had failed to follow the process laid down by the Union home ministry for such deportations.

item.title: How ‘new’ is the tilcayo, the first cat species to be discovered in a 100 years?
item.description: Researchers knew of a tiger cat occurred in Bolivia’s Yungas cloud forests, but it had never been formally described.
item.content:encoded:
Scientists have described a species of tiger cat that was previously unknown to science. From Bolivia’s Yungas cloud forests, it is the first discovery of a living novel cat species in more than 100 years.

The tilcayo (Leopardus tilcayo) takes its species name from the name locals already had for it. Paola Nogales-Ascarrunz, a National Geographic explorer who discovered the species and co-author of the Current Biology paper that describes it, said the name honors traditional knowledge in the region.

The tilcayo is smaller than a domestic cat at 1.4 kilograms (3 pounds). It has rounded ears, a slender body and a coat with large spots.

“I have the honor of naming a cat, and that’s a really big thing,” Nogales-Ascarrunz, who is also a researcher at the Universidad Mayor de San Andrés in La Paz, Bolivia, told Mongabay by phone.

For decades, researchers lumped small spotted cats across South America under a single species name: Leopardus tigrinus or tiger cat. However, evidence had been mounting for years that the group might contain several species.

In the article published on September 17, researchers unwound the species’ genetic web and confirmed at least four distinct species.

item.title: Punjab: Two arrested for allegedly spreading rumours of girls missing from university hostel
item.description: The two persons who were detained are former students, police said.
item.content:encoded:
The Punjab Police on Friday arrested two persons for allegedly provoking students of Chitkara University to protest by spreading rumours on social media that two women students had gone missing from the institute’s hostel, The Indian Express reported.

The unrest at the private university began on the night of September 25 after rumours circulated on social media that two students had gone missing from their hostel.

The students allegedly damaged two police vehicles and assaulted a police officer during the protest. They also alleged that the officer was under the influence of alcohol when he reached the campus to control the situation.

On Friday, Patiala Senior Superintendent of Police Harmandeep Singh Hans said the arrested persons, Himanshu and Aryan, were former students of the university, The Indian Express reported. They allegedly incited students by spreading misleading messages in multiple social media groups.

They have been booked under sections of the Bharatiya Nyay Sanhita pertaining to attempt to murder, wrongful confinement, obstructing a public servant, assault on a public servant, criminal intimidation, wrongful restraint, disturbing public peace, rioting, unlawful assembly and criminal conspiracy, the newspaper reported.

The first information report was registered on September 29, and police are trying to apprehend 10 other persons named in the FIR, the officer said.

item.title: The reason for Indian democracy’s downslide is collapse of judiciary: Indira Jaising
item.description: ‘Sons of judges are judges, the judiciary makes no apologies for being dynastic.’
item.content:encoded:
Few people know more about India’s courts than Indira Jaising. In a career spanning more than half a century, Jaising has practised both at the Bombay High Court and the Supreme Court.

On this episode of ‘Scroll Adda’, she speaks to Shoaib Daniyal on the ills plaguing the judiciary. Dynasty has taken over the courts, she says, leading to a lack of intellectual development. Bright young lawyers without family contacts are forced to leave litigation.

The judiciary is not doing its job of being a check on the executive. Jaising argues that this government is simply ignoring the Constitution and the courts are unable to stop it. ‘The reason for Indian democracy’s downslide is the collapse of the judiciary,’ she says.

Meanwhile, public movements like the Jantar Mantar protests, sparked by the Chief Justice’s “cockroach” comment, show that anger against the judiciary is boiling over into the streets.

item.title: ‘Nothing imminent’: US official on trade deal with India
item.description: Jamieson Greer said Donald Trump and Narendra Modi may have another phone call soon to assess the progress on the negotiations.
item.content:encoded:
United States Trade Representative Jamieson Greer on Thursday said that India and the US were nearing the end of negotiations for a trade deal, but added that an agreement was not imminent as the two sides had identified a “universe of items that are sticking points”, ANI reported.

“We are continually trying to finish the trade deal with India…,” he said.

Greer’s remarks came a day after he met Union Minister of Commerce and Industry Piyush Goyal during the G20 Trade Ministers’ Meeting in Milwaukee, Wisconsin. The US is hosting the G20 this year.

Greer described his conversation with Goyal as “very constructive”.

“At the same time, I do not think there is something imminent, but we truly have identified the universe of items that are sticking points,” ANI quoted him as saying. “We are working diligently towards them.”

Greer also said US President Donald Trump and Prime Minister Narendra Modi could speak again “very soon” to assess progress of the trade deal.

On Wednesday, Modi and Trump reviewed progress in bilateral cooperation, including trade, defence, energy and critical technologies, the Ministry of External Affairs said.

A Hindu religious group whose visit to the Eiffel Tower last month triggered a controversy said on Thursday that an investigation had established that it did not ask for women staff to be removed from the Paris landmark.

The statement came after the General Inspectorate of the City of Paris found that there had been “no explicit request” from the delegation to remove women, AFP reported.

On September 7, staff at the monument went on a brief strike to protest the removal of women colleagues during the BAPS delegation visit, two days earlier.

The removal of the women staff sparked criticism from French politicians across the political spectrum, who said the country’s commitment to gender equality was non-negotiable.

On Tuesday, the company that manages the Eiffel Tower said its chief would step down in the wake of the controversy.

Patrick Branco Ruivo will leave his role at the end of the year after an internal probe found “operational flaws and shortcomings” in organising the visit that had led to the “unacceptable” removal of women staff.

Geetanjali Shree’s Our City That Year, translated by Daisy Rockwell from the original 1998 Hindi novel Hamara Shahar Us Baras, is one of the 13 books longlisted for the 10th annual award of the £1000 Warwick Prize for Women in Translation in 2026.

Rockwell and Shree were co-winners of the prize in 2022 for the International Booker Prize winner Tomb of Sand, translated from the original Hindi novel Ret Samadhi (with Osebol: Voices from a Swedish Village by Marit Kapla, translated from the Swedish by Peter Graves).

The prize was established by the University of Warwick in 2017 to address the gender imbalance in translated literature and to increase the number of international women’s voices especially among British and Irish readers.

This year, the competition received a total of 164 eligible entries representing 37 languages, the highest so far. The longlist covers 12 languages and includes fiction, poetry, short stories, and narrative non-fiction. The jury comprises Arifa Akbar, Véronique Tadjo, and Boyd Tonkin.

item.title: ‘I brought her up with such loving care’: Tagore writes about missing his daughter after marriage
item.description: An excerpt from ‘Tagore: An Illustrated Biography’, by Uma Das Gupta.
item.content:encoded:
In one of his letters to his wife, Mrinalini Devi, Rabindranath wrote:

I do constantly try not to worry about our children. It is our duty to see to it that they are well-behaved and that they get a good education. Beyond that it is a mistake to torture our minds over them. They will grow up to do their life’s work in their own way whether good, bad, or indifferent. They are our children, true, but they are also individual in their own right. We shall not exercise control over the way they live their lives.

Let us do our duty by them but let us not expect too much from them. How they shall turn out as human beings is in God’s hands. Expecting and imagining that my child shall be the best of all is the product of a certain vanity. I have no right to do that. So many other children have hard lives, do we feel concerned for them?

Like a protective mother, Mrinalini Devi used to worry over how their daughter Bela was doing after her marriage. To reassure her, Rabindranath visited Bela at her husband’s home and wrote that he found her doing well.

item.title: ‘#Love’ review: Ample chemistry smoothens out the creases in the writing
item.description: Balaji Mohan’s Netflix series stars Aishwarya Lekshmi and Arjun Das.
item.content:encoded:
Balaji Mohan’s six-episode Tamil series on Netflix sets up a wager between chemistry and compatibility. What makes two people fall in love: chemistry or compatibility?

#Love gives the familiar romantic question a contemporary spin through dating apps, algorithms and start-up culture. The result is breezy viewing that raises potentially interesting questions about how we connect.

Written by Nirmal Williams along with Sharada Subramanian and Shweta Chakravarty, the series revolves around two competing dating apps. Tara (Aishwarya Lekshmi), the self-made founder of Found, believes that relationships are built on compatibility. Matthew (Arjun Das), a wealthy investor and adventure junkie, backs Find My Bae, which puts chemistry first.

Their opposing philosophies become personal when they embark on a 60-day challenge to settle the debate over whether harmony or hormones is more essential to an ideal match.

It is a neat premise. Can compatibility be reduced to an AI-generated score? Can an algorithm account for the unpredictable ways people connect? Does chemistry survive the realities of everyday life? The romcom raises these questions, but rarely stays with them long enough to make them meaningful.

item.title: Futile for Indians to believe they are ‘Aryans’: How Gandhi inspired Du Bois to reimagine the world
item.description: The African-American scholar had a long engagement with India and drew on the freedom struggle to forge a grounds for solidarity among people of colour.
item.content:encoded:
In 1936, the African American scholar and activist WEB Du Bois wrote an article for The Aryan Path, a magazine published out of Mumbai that advocated Theosophical views but also carried articles on contemporary political events and philosophical ideas. The magazine was edited by BP Wadia, a Theosophist and a trade unionist.

The editors had asked Du Bois to write an article about the special features of African American culture. Du Bois asked if he could instead write about “The Methods of Increasing the Interest and Knowledge between Indians and American Negroes”. He titled the article “The Clash of Colour”.

Nearly a century later, his observations sound very contemporary. The difficulty in establishing any relationship between Indians and African Americans, he argued, lay “in the almost utter lack of knowledge which these two groups of people have of each other”. American schools taught very little of Indian history, and educated Indians tended to believe American and English propaganda about African Americans.

item.title: From Azad Hind Radio to Gandhi: The forgotten Indian story of Surinamese composer Majoie Hajary
item.description: The pianist with Indian roots moved from wartime radio and New Delhi to ragas, devotional music and one of the most unusual Gandhi recordings of the 1960s.
item.content:encoded:
Any serious conversation about Gandhi and music would be incomplete without discussing a French record from 1968. Requiem pour Mahatma Gandhi was composed by Majoie Hajary, who was born in Suriname, trained in Amsterdam and Paris, spent time in New Delhi and moved throughout her life between musical worlds that others had preferred to keep apart.

Hajary was born in 1921 in Paramaribo, capital of the Dutch colony of Suriname in South America. While her father was born in Suriname, her paternal grandparents had come from India. Her mother was Afro-Chinese. Her ancestors had come to the colony as indentured labourers.

Hajary grew up in comfort, principally with Western classical music at home.

Ellen de Vries, author of the 2025 Hajary biography Surinaamse Rapsodie and the researcher behind a website about the composer, majoiehajary.org, helped fill in some of the gaps in Hajary’s Indian story.

In an email message, de Vries said that 15-year-old Hajary left for Amsterdam in 1937 to study at the conservatory, already carrying more than one musical language with her. Her interest in Indian music deepened in the Dutch capital, and later through encounters with Indian musicians and teachers in Berlin in Germany and Caracas in Venezuela.

item.title: ‘Drishyam The Conclusion’ review: Vijay Salgaonkar faces a new adversary – but barely
item.description: Abhishek Pathak’s thriller pits Ajay Devgn against Jaideep Ahlawat.
item.content:encoded:
Jeethu Joseph’s Drishyam films have yielded remakes in several languages, most profitably in Hindi. The Bollywood versions are led by Ajay Devgn, stepping into the role immortalised by Mohanlal – of the barely educated, devoted family man who comes up with a brilliant alibi to save his wife and older daughter from a murder rap. item.title: The start of a run can feel like a fight against your body – and that is normal
item.description: This sensation is actually caused by a normal feature of human physiology.
item.content:encoded:
Many runners describe the first ten to 15 minutes of a run as the hardest of all. Breathing can feel laboured, the legs can feel heavy and a pace that would normally seem manageable may suddenly feel surprisingly difficult.

It might be easy to assume the reason your run feels so difficult at the start is because you’re not fit enough. But in reality, this sensation is actually caused by a normal feature of human physiology – and one that affects almost everyone, from someone attempting their first 5K to elite endurance athletes.

One way I often explain this phenomenon to athletes and students is that when you begin running, an argument starts between your muscles and your cardiorespiratory system. While there’s nothing we can do to stop this quarrel from happening, there are many things we can do to help the body find a resolution more quickly in the future.

The moment you start running, your working muscles demand a rapid supply of energy almost instantly. Yet the system responsible for producing that energy from oxygen cannot respond quite as quickly.

A 43-year-old Muslim fish trader from West Bengal’s Uttar Dinajpur district was picked up by Raiganj Police for being an allegedly undocumented Bangladeshi immigrant and pushed into Bangladesh, his family told Scroll.

The police had detained Abdul Barek, a resident of Gopalpur village, in June.

The man also has an Indian passport issued in 2021. Scroll has seen the voter list, his voter identity card and a copy of the passport.

item.title: Rohingya genocide: ICJ will soon issue ruling on case against Myanmar

item.content:encoded:
The International Court of Justice is reportedly going to rule in the coming weeks in The Gambia v. Myanmar, the genocide case against Myanmar.

In 2019, The Gambia filed an application at the ICJ alleging that Myanmar had violated the United Nations’ 1948 Genocide Convention in its treatment of the Rohingya people.

The Rohingya aren’t from The Gambia, and no atrocities against them took place there. But, under international law, any state can file a case with the ICJ if it believes a country has violated the convention. This was confirmed by the court in a 2022 decision against Myanmar’s attempt to block the case on jurisdictional grounds.

Who are the Rohingya?

The Rohingya are an ethnic minority group that have long lived in the Arakan region of western Myanmar, which today corresponds to the Rakhine state.

As Muslims in an overwhelmingly Buddhist country, the Rohingya have often experienced discrimination and persecution. Most notably, in 1982, Myanmar passed a law that removed the Rohingya from a list of ethnic groups eligible for citizenship.

As a result, most Rohingya lost their citizenship, and with it, their most basic rights and freedoms. The ICJ case, however, concerns the campaign of violence conducted by the Myanmar military against the Rohingya that began in 2016.

Reading news reports in recent weeks has made one thing clear: being a Bengali-speaking Muslim has, by itself, become incriminating in today’s India.

Simply having this ethno-linguistic identity is enough to trigger the suspicion of state officials. Amid the fervid political rhetoric about “ghuspetiya” – infiltrators – and supposed demographic change, being a Bengali-speaking Muslim has come to be associated with being an outsider.

Across the country, Bengali-speaking Muslim marginal workers are being picked up for questioning, detained and even deported to Bangladesh. For instance, last month in Bengaluru, 3,000-odd Bengali Muslim garbage and waste workers were picked up by the police as part of a massive verification drive against allegedly unauthorised migrants.

The assault took place as worshipers gathered for Friday prayers in the city of Kohat, in Khyber Puktunkhwa province, northwest Pakistan. item.description: Deleting voters before verification ‘is a heinous offence’ and the chief election commissioner is guilty of that, alleged former BJP leader RK Singh.
item.content:encoded:
Former Union minister RK Singh on Monday alleged that Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar “and his bosses” were violating the law through the manner in which they were conducting the special intensive revision of electoral rolls.

Singh said that the order to conduct the SIR across the country was illegal as section 21 of the 1950 Representation of the People Act says that the exercise can be undertaken only in specific cases, “for reasons to be recorded in writing in each case; and that also only in any constituency or part of a constituency”.

An exception allowed for special cases cannot become a rule, he said on social media. “The Supreme Court order upholding the general SIR was wrong,” he added.

Singh said that the Union government and the Election Commission’s efforts have always been to enrol all eligible voters to deepen democracy. “This is the first time in the history of the country that the mission is to disenfranchise people,” he added.

Singh was a minister in the Narendra Modi government between 2019 and 2024. He was the Union home secretary between 2011 and 2013 in the Manmohan Singh government.

He resigned from the Bharatiya Janata Party in November after he was suspended for alleged activities against the party.

item.title: SC says ‘no question’ of examining Amit Shah’s discharge in Sohrabuddin Sheikh case
item.description: The bench sought responses from 22 persons, including 21 police personnel, who were acquitted in the matter and the Central Bureau of Investigation.
item.content:encoded:
The Supreme Court on Monday said that there was “no question” of examining any challenge to the discharge of Union Home Minister Amit Shah in the alleged staged “encounter” killings of Sohrabuddin Sheikh and his aide Tulsiram Prajapati, and the alleged murder of Sohrabuddin Sheikh’s wife Kauser Bi in Gujarat, reported Bar and Bench.

Hearing an appeal by Rubabuddin Sheikh, the brother of Sohrabuddin Sheikh, the court sought responses from the Central Bureau of Investigation and 22 persons, including 21 police personnel, who had been accused in the case.

Rubabuddin Sheikh has challenged the Bombay High Court’s May 7 decision to uphold the acquittal of the 22 persons accused in the case.

Sohrabuddin Sheikh, who was a wanted criminal, was killed by the Gujarat Police in November 2005 in an “encounter”, which is alleged to have been staged. He and his wife were travelling by bus from Hyderabad to Sangli in Maharashtra when they were stopped by the Gujarat and Rajasthan police, allegedly abducted and shot dead near Gandhinagar.

A sub-inspector also allegedly raped Kauser Bi before murdering her. Prajapati was the sole witness to the murders. He was in police custody after the incident but was shot dead in another “encounter” in December 2006, when the police claimed he was trying to escape.

item.title: Conflict of interest concerns follow CEC Gyanesh Kumar from Sambhal to the Supreme Court
item.description: The Election Commission dismissed complaints of voter suppression in Sambhal based on a report by returning officer Manish Bansal, Gyanesh Kumar’s son-in-law.
item.content:encoded:
Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar is facing scrutiny over key decisions taken without the knowledge and consent of fellow election commissioners, as revealed in an investigation by The Indian Express.

There are also questions of conflict of interest over relief granted to Kumar’s daughter, Noida District Magistrate Medha Roopam, by a Supreme Court bench led by Justice Satish Chandra Sharma. The judge’s son serves as standing counsel for the poll body in Madhya Pradesh, reported LiveLaw.

This is not the first time that concerns about conflict of interest have surfaced around Kumar and his family.

On May 7, 2024, video footage showed Muslim voters being forced out of several polling stations in Sambhal, Uttar Pradesh, while the Lok Sabha election was underway.

Many of these voters were women, who told Scroll that police officials had assaulted them to prevent them from voting.

But the Election Commission did not act on these complaints. Instead, it came out in support of a statement by the returning officer and labelled the damning footage as “false” and “misleading”.

The returning officer overseeing the polls in Sambhal was district magistrate Manish Bansal – the son-in-law of Gyanesh Kumar, then serving as an election commissioner.

item.title: Should England be charging a tourism tax?
item.description: A well-implemented visitor levy can indeed have a positive effect on the tourism industry but there are many nuances to consider.
item.content:encoded:
Supporters tend to call it a “visitor levy”. Detractors prefer to call it a “tourist tax”.

Whether you agree with it or not, an extra charge for overnight stays has become a common feature of modern travel. Recent visitors to New York, Prague, Milan and Edinburgh will have already paid it. And now mayors in England will have the chance to impose it.

Some think these fees will cause huge damage to the hospitality sector, while adding to the general cost of living for visitors. But the main argument in favour of the charge is that it is a simple way of raising much-needed revenue.

A report I worked on for the Welsh government showed that a well-implemented visitor levy can indeed have a positive effect on the tourism industry.

Looking at destinations in Italy, Iceland, Spain and the US, the evidence suggested that a tourism tax can bring benefits to the local community while also improving sustainability, by funding environmental projects, for example.

But getting it implemented turns out to be far from simple. There are key elements which have to be decided upon, and different places – big cities and coastal towns, for example – need different approaches.

item.description: The CEC’s actions related to the voter roll revision were ‘serious infringement’ of constitutional functioning, the Constitutional Conduct Group said.
item.content:encoded:
A group of former bureaucrats on Monday demanded the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar for alleged irregularities in the conduct of special intensive revision of electoral rolls in the country.

In an open letter, the Constitutional Conduct Group said that the Election Commission’s functioning has become “imperious, autocratic and dictatorial” because of Kumar. It added that his actions around the SIR exercise represented “serious infringement” of constitutional functioning and legality.

On Saturday, the group had called on the Election Commission to scrap the special intensive revision of electoral rolls.

The letter came amid similar demands by the Opposition and civil society groups for Kumar’s removal over alleged irregularities in the functioning of the poll panel. The demands came after The Indian Express reported on Wednesday that two election commissioners had objected to decisions related to the SIR.

The newspaper’s investigation showed that Election Commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi had formally objected 14 times in 10 months to the poll panel’s decisions about the SIR, saying that some had been taken without their knowledge.

The bench took note of a settlement reached between the Shahi Masjid Waqf Panch Mochiyan and the Ujjain Municipal Corporation. The details of the settlement were not placed before the court.

However, the demolition of part of the mosque is underway, the police said.

item.description: An excerpt from ‘Suddenly the Moon’, by Anirudh Acharya.
item.content:encoded:
1

Playing by itself
with an abandoned slipper —

the evening sea

2

In the open night
the attar on my wrist too
smells of the moon

3

Much to say to you
not in front of the others —
my eyes tell the moon

4

She wipes her brow
with the back of her hand —
ãttã in her hair

5

Candlelight dinner
Needing a phone’s light to
Look at the menu

6

The only sign
of autumn’s coming —
“End of Season” sale

7

Suddenly the moon —
out over the vast ocean
rain clouds drifting by

8

In this well-lived home
even by the old kitchen sink
fond memories

9

Deep in the mountains
surrounded by many trees —
joy of learning names

Midday at the beach —
lovers snuggle closer-in
quickly shrinking shade

Lost to the city
but here in this tiny lane —
chirping of sparrows

Again fresh flowers
on the road leading
to the burning ground

Sleepy afternoon —
white spots on an orange cat
filled in by sunlight


At the beach
people sit facing the sea
to look into phones

At every turn
street dogs ask with erect ears
“Who are you?”

item.title: Hardy crops are failing in drought-hit parts of Karnataka
item.description: There has been a decline in ragi and millet kharif sowing area.
item.content:encoded:
Shiva Shekhar, a 40-year-old farmer from Padavalapatna village in Mandya district’s Nagamangala taluk, could not sow ragi this kharif. “I kept waiting for the rain but it never came, so I sowed cowpea instead, which is more drought-tolerant,” he said on September 16.

Karnataka is the largest ragi-producing state in the country. In 2025-’26, India produced 2 million tonnes of ragi, of which 1.47 million tonnes came from Karnataka, according to the Third Advance Estimates for the year from the Department of Agriculture and Farmers Welfare. The state also accounted for about 73% of the area under ragi that year, at 979,000 hectares. Of that, Mandya –located about 40 km north of Mysuru – accounted for about 53,300 hectares.

Broadly, ragi sowing at the national and state levels has kept pace with last year. But in Mandya, against a target of 63,385 hectare for this year, ragi was sown in 1,213 hectare (1.91%) by September 11, data shared by Jayaswamy, joint director of agriculture for Mandya, show.

By September 11, Karnataka had an overall decline of 1.5 million hectares in kharif sowing area compared to last year. Of this, roughly a third each was in paddy, and the broad category of millets and coarse cereals.

item.title: J&K passes Omar Abdullah’s statehood resolution amid walkout by BJP
item.description: Bharatiya Janata Party MLAs objected to a reference to the 2000 autonomy resolution in the new one.
item.content:encoded:
The Jammu and Kashmir Assembly on Monday passed a resolution, moved by Chief Minister Omar Abdullah, seeking statehood for the Union Territory amid protests by Bharatiya Janata Party legislators, The Hindu reported.

While the Congress and the Peoples Democratic Party MLAs supported the move, the BJP legislators shouted slogans against it over its reference to the resolution passed by the Assembly in 2000.

In June 2000, the National Conference government led by Farooq Abdullah passed a resolution in the Assembly calling for restoration of greater autonomy to Jammu and Kashmir as it existed before August 1953. However, it was rejected by the then-Atal Bihari Vajpayee government at the Centre.

The text of the fresh resolution moved by Abdullah on Friday says that in addition to the resolutions passed by the Assembly in June 2000 and November 2024, the House was calling on the Union government to urgently restore Jammu and Kashmir’s statehood.

In November 2024, the Assembly passed another resolution calling for the restoration of the special status the erstwhile state had under Article 370 of the Constitution, which was abrogated by the Union government in August 2019.

He returned from the bakery earlier than usual that afternoon, a black thundercloud still tethered to his big bullet head. His common-law wife caught the mood, did not probe, and took off on her own to catch the 4 pm show at Ganga Talkies right next door. Adi paced and kicked furniture listlessly, waiting for his son Cyrus to pop in for ritual Saturday sundowners at 6 pm.

“The weather is going nuts,” huffed Cyrus cheerfully, bang on time, airing out a moist, sticky T-shirt as he sank into his designated spot on the vermilion-coloured sofa.

item.title: SC refuses to stay fee on UPI payments above Rs 2,000
item.description: However, the bench asked the Union government to explain the decision to allow the charges.
item.content:encoded:
The Supreme Court on Monday refused to stay the Union government’s decision to allow fee to be levied on Unified Payments Interface transactions above Rs 2,000, Live Law reported.

However, the court sought the government’s response on the petition challenging the move.

On September 14 and September 15, the Ministry of Finance issued notifications stating that UPI payments to merchants valued above Rs 2,000 would attract a merchant discount rate of 0.4%.

Merchant discount rate is a fee charged to businesses by banks to cover the costs of processing transactions. The rate typically ranges from 1% to 3% of the transaction value for credit card payments and can be up to 0.9% for debit card transactions.

The petitioner submitted before the court that businesses may pass on the additional cost of the UPI charges to consumers.

Additional Solicitor General N Venkataraman, appearing for the Union government, submitted before the court that 96% of transactions would not attract the charge, Live Law reported. The charges would take effect on October 15.

“It is neither a tax nor a fee,” he was quoted as saying.

Chief Justice Surya Kant said that the government should place these facts on an affidavit as “it is more of a technical issue”, the legal news outlet reported.

With bye-elections in the Rejinagar and Nandigram Assembly constituencies scheduled for October 6, a mention was made before a bench led by Chief Justice Surya Kant seeking an earlier hearing.

A counsel had verbally mentioned that the case had been listed for Tuesday but had not appeared on. the cause list.

item.title: SC says recent Delhi rape cases show failure of police, administration; takes suo moto cognisance
item.description: There have been at least 13 cases of sexual assault in the national capital this month.
item.content:encoded:
The Supreme Court on Monday took suo moto cognisance of a spate of rape cases in Delhi, saying it underlined a “systematic failure” of the law enforcement authorities and the administration to guarantee basic public safety, Live Law reported.

At least 13 cases of sexual assault have been reported in Delhi this month, The Print reported.

These include the gang rape of a 17-year-old allegedly by three men who posed as police personnel in a park near Lady Shri Ram College on September 21.

On September 13, the body of a 16-year-old girl was found decomposed in Swaroop Nagar, two days after she was allegedly raped and murdered, The Hindu reported.

On August 4, a 17-year-old was gang raped by a bus driver and conductor inside a moving bus as it covered a distance of nearly 47 km from Greater Noida to Kashmere Gate without being checked at any police picket, The Indian Express reported.

On Monday, the bench of Justices JB Pardiwala and K Vinod Chandran said that they were distressed by these reports and highlighted the need to fix accountability.

While referring to the August 4 case, the bench said that “one cannot help but draw painful parallels to the Nirbhaya incident of 2012”.
